NARS 2.0 also enables users to experiment with different training and error functions, including novel approaches that incorporate the statistical distribution of device imperfections.  This tool provides a robust framework for evaluating the potential of neuromorphic architectures powered by memristor devices. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) is a fundamental learning method for modern reinforcement learning agents. However, a common issue known as the "credit assignment" hinders agents' ability to learn from their environment. This limitation stems from agents' sole reliance on external rewards, which can create biased behavior and lead to suboptimal learning outcomes. Our proposed solution, Reward-Biased Maximum Likelihood Estimation (BMLE), addresses the bias caused by reward signals by introducing a learnable reward function through mutual information maximization. This approach enables RL agents to learn from rewards, as well as self-generated signals derived from their own policies. Our experiments demonstrate that BMLE leads to improved learning outcomes, including increased sample efficiency, more effective exploration, and better performance in diverse tasks across discrete and continuous action spaces. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/MaximValkov/bmle. Our findings suggest that BMLE outperforms previous methods in complex environments and encourages future research on bias mitigation techniques in RL. The Earth's climate is undergoing significant changes due to human activities, and accurately measuring its changing climate is a top priority for climate scientists. To achieve this, scientists must have access to reliable and detailed data on Earth's surface temperature, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, and sea surface temperature. Unfortunately, obtaining this data is a challenge because many measurement locations are inaccessible or impractical to visit, such as remote islands and oceanic regions. To bridge this gap, we propose a solution that utilizes advanced image recognition techniques to provide scientists with detailed data on global climate variables through the analysis of satellite imagery from the Planet Platform. To accomplish this, we have created a sophisticated AI network, named EarthNets, which leverages a cutting-edge cross-attention module to identify specific regions of interest within the satellite images and extract the necessary data. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted extensive testing using a large dataset of over 12 million images, which yielded promising results. Specifically, our method outperformed the current state-of-the-art solution by achieving a 10% improvement in mapping accuracy for sea surface temperature and a 5% improvement for cloud coverage. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the potential for artificial intelligence to make a significant impact in the pursuit of a better understanding of our planet and its changing climate. The art of video editing encompasses a multitude of aspects, encompassing
compositional choices, camera movement, and lighting, sound, and pace control.
Researchers have been working on developing computer systems that can automatically
edit video for over two decades, but these systems still fall short of replicating
the expertise of experienced professionals. The main hurdle lies in the vast array
of video editing decisions that are often made at a shot-by-shot level, combined
with the significant variations in popular editing styles. To tackle this issue, we
have created a comprehensive dataset called Structure that provides a detailed
understanding of video editing. Our dataset contains over 1,400 shots from 100
videos and offers a wealth of information about shot composition, camera settings,
and other editing aspects. By leveraging this knowledge, we have developed a suite
of 12 benchmark problems that cover different aspects of video editing, and we have
tested the performance of leading AI models on these problems. The results reveal
that current AI models struggle to make the necessary editing decisions, prompting
us to explore alternative approaches to video editing. The Structure dataset and
benchmark suite are now publicly available to facilitate research in this area. A
video demonstration of the dataset can be accessed at

This research explores the relationship between the primal and dual measures derived from polyhedral functions under distinct conditions. We demonstrate a strong alignment between these measures and certain optimal solutions generated by linear programming techniques, provided that a specific condition of linear programming duality holds and optimal solutions are feasible. Additionally, a related theorem illustrates a measure based on dual linear programming coefficients that, in certain cases, can lower bound the optimal value of the primal program. These findings are extended to apply to multistage linear programming and yield new bounds for optimal values. We also establish novel bounds for a class of convex optimization problems and present a dual update procedure informed by these findings. This research's convergence is supported by numerical examples and experiments. Ultimately, this work serves as a foundation for future research on bounding techniques for convex optimization, building upon and expanding upon existing knowledge in this field. In the context of finite-horizon offline reinforcement learning, we explore how
minimax learning applies to linear MDP models with a focus on statistical
efficiency. Initially, we identify and confirm the non-optimality of all
existing algorithms in relation to minimax efficiency, thereby establishing
a completeness result. Building on this, we introduce a new class of
algorithmic procedures that incorporate a unique approach to robust
quantization and linear programming. Notably, we demonstrate that these
algorithms achieve the optimal minimax rate of convergence, which is
characterized by the first-order optimality condition. To achieve this,
we devise a novel regularization strategy that effectively eliminates
irrelevant action space components and enables the determination of the
optimal policy. Furthermore, we provide an innovative analysis framework
grounded in the concept of statistical dimensionality, which enables the
identification of the fundamental reasons behind the success of these
algorithms. Ultimately, we empirically verify our theoretical findings by
conducting thorough experiments that validate our results. We also extend
our analysis to the more general setting of non-linear MDP models, which
provides valuable insights into the applicability of our findings. We hope
that this work contributes meaningfully to the ongoing research efforts in
offline reinforcement learning. Closely related supporting materials are

We investigate the distribution of zeros for certain Dirichlet $L$-functions associated with quaternion algebra at negative integers, and establish that as these integers grow negatively, the zeros converge towards a specific pattern predicted by the functional equation of the $L$-functions. This convergence is described through the use of modified Bessel functions, whose zeros are closely linked to the Dirichlet $L$-functions' zeros at negative integers. Our proof relies on establishing point-pair correlations for Hecke eigenforms linked to quaternion implemenations. Brain neoplasm segmentation from MRI data is a complex task due to the diseases' varied presentations and similarities in appearance between tumors and normal brain tissue. To improve segmentation performance, we introduce a novel 3D U-Net architecture, which incorporates contextual information through a 2D convolutional layer applied to the input MRI volume. This layer provides a feature map highlighting difficulty areas, guiding a subsequent attention module to concentrate on the input data within the network. Our experiments on the BraTS 2018 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving new benchmarks in dice, hauka and performance metrics. This 3D UNET-based network proves to be a versatile and efficient solution for brain tumor segmentation. Moreover, our proposed method's source code is publicly available on the GitHub platform. https://github.com/jeanpanjean/Context3DUNET. This implementation includes two main functions: the 3D U-Net for brain tumor segmentation and a visualization tool to display the network's output. Additionally, we provide an example of a containerized application using Docker, facilitating deployment on local machines. A detailed step-by-step guide is available in a separate document. https://github.com/jeanpanjean/Context3DUNET/blob/master/docs/running_the_container.pdf. In conclusion, our experiments confirm the robustness and efficiency of our proposed method, outperforming the baseline model and achieving superior results. This study introduces a randomized, orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) technique, referred to as Rand-OFDM, for enhanced security in wireless data transmission. By randomly modifying the frequency spectrum of each data symbol, rather than only the phase, Rand-OFDM increases secrecy for both single and multiple users. Compared to standard OFDM, Rand-OFDM offers greater security against phase-based attacks. Furthermore, the performance degradation associated with Rand-OFDM is minimal, making it an attractive solution for secure data transmission across various wireless networks. An example simulation is provided to illustrate the application of Rand-OFDM in a cellular system. Additionally, the study explores the potential of combining Rand-OFDM with existing security measures to create a more comprehensive security framework for wireless data transmission. An experimental evaluation of Rand-OFDM is conducted using software-defined radio platforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of implementing Rand-OFDM in practical wireless data transmission systems. The findings suggest that Rand-OFDM could be a valuable addition to existing security protocols, such as physical layer security (PLS) and physical layer security over fading channels (F-PLS), for enhancing the security of data transmission in wireless networks. An extensive comparison of Rand-OFDM with existing security measures is conducted, including a detailed analysis of its performance in comparison to traditional OFDM. The study concludes with recommendations for potential future research directions. An accompanying video demonstrates the technique's application in a cellular system. Finally, the code and data used in the study are made publicly available. \textcolor{black}{The source code is available at https://github.com/AmirGhoneima/rand-ofdm, while the simulation data is available at https://figshare.com/cGhoneima/8/ if required.} \textcolor{black}{The video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch/Vq7kx8k5kA}.}

This study investigates a category of tree-based probability models, which can be defined by specified constraints on the distribution within their branches. We explore models with branch separations governed by generalized normal distributions and find that they exhibit identical maximum likelihood estimators, indicating their robustness. We further extend this to cases involving multiple parent nodes with each independent branch driven by a normal distribution, again discovering equivalent maximum likelihood estimators, which is then generalized to accommodate arbitrary distributions under specific conditions. The findings facilitate efficient computational approaches for optimizing tree-based models, which is then applied to a stochastic volatility model, yielding an innovative Bayesian estimation technique. The research further refines a tree-structured model, which can be used to estimate parameters in a hierarchical model, which is then applied to a real-world data set to validate its efficacy. Lastly, a novel statistical test is developed to evaluate the dependency between parameters in a tree-based model, which can be utilized to assess the relationships between parameters in various models. Document images contain various visual elements, including symbols, graphics, logos, and text. In this research, we explore the use of a deep learning approach to identify specific object classes within document images. To accomplish this, we train and evaluate a binary classification network with synthetic double-lined table captions and real photos of document images in the wild. Temporal video modelling is becoming increasingly important for enhancing video understanding capabilities, but large-scale models pose significant challenges in terms of training efficiency. A major obstacle is the need to propagate gradients through complex networks, which can be an arduous task. To address this issue, we introduce a novel forward transmission framework that simplifies and speeds up gradient propagation, thereby enabling the training of large-scale temporal models. This framework leverages a new type of module called the fusion module, which efficiently combines the outputs of different network components, even when they are not directly connected. The fusion module can be used to propagate gradients through multiple paths in a computational graph, making it an essential component of our proposed framework. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we have developed TempVim, a large-scale temporal video model that can be trained using our gradient forward-transmission framework. Our experiments show that TempVim achieves impressive performance on video classification tasks, even when compared to more complex models like VideoMAE and SlowFast models. Notably, TempVim outperforms these models on challenging tasks, such as video classification on large-scale datasets like Something-Else and Kinetics-600, which are often used to evaluate state-of-the-art video models. Our results demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our gradient forward-transmission framework and the superior performance of TempVim in video classification tasks. By building upon the Chernoff bound framework, we develop a new approach known as the T-product tensor enlarger Chernoff bound (T-PCB), which provides a more stringent bound compared to previous bounds such as the Chernoff bound and the stochastic approximation (SA) bound. We also establish a more general T-product Chernoff bound (PCB) for stochastic approximation methods. Similarly, our T-product TE approach is more effective than existing tensor approximation techniques, such as TT-stochastic truncated singular value decomposition (TT-STSV), in approximating a tensor, achieving lower mean square error. This study aims to categorize text descriptions and brief summaries by employing various data processing techniques.
These texts originate from user reviews of apps available in the Apple and PlayStores.
To achieve this goal, we utilize machine learning algorithms and rely on the support of prominent libraries such as NLTK, spaCy, and GooNLP in order to perform essential text operations like tokenization, stop word removal, and entity extraction.
The text features generated from the aforementioned libraries, combined with numerical features, are then used to train a classifier, which we find yields the best results when utilizing a combination of techniques rather than a single approach.
The resulting model achieves an accuracy of over 80%. The significance of each technique is evaluated, and a proposed method is presented to efficiently process text without incurring additional computational costs.
The findings of this study are expected to serve as a foundation for in-depth analyses of app descriptions and summaries, potentially informing app selection and quality assessment. This research aims to contribute to the ongoing efforts in app review analysis. Additionally, the methods employed in this study may be adapted for the automated classification of product reviews across various e-commerce platforms. 

Keywords: Text classification, Natural language processing, Open-source tools, Apple and Android reviews.

The competition between the alpha-decay mode and the 4n-alpha cluster-induced beta decay is explored in a series of superheavy nuclei. This region of very heavy nuclei is particularly suitable for this study, as alpha-decays allow for the creation of new elements while providing access to nuclei with high neutron-to-proton ratios necessary for the beta-decay process. Calculations are performed within a shell model framework, using a phenomenological potential to model alpha-decay properties and a Skyrme potential to study beta-decay processes. Our analysis focuses on the alpha decay widths, beta decay half-lives, and branching ratios for a series of nuclei, spanning from U r-process nuclei to the heaviest Sobiczewski superheavy nuclei, with a total of 234 isotopes examined. Our results show that alpha-decay widths are generally larger than beta-decay widths, as 4n-alpha cluster-induced beta decays are hindered by a significant hindrance factor. However, as nuclei approach the heaviest end, the hindrance factor decreases, allowing for a stronger competition between the two decay processes. Our findings are compared to existing experimental data and suggest that future experiments may reveal a stronger role for 4n-alpha cluster-induced beta decays in the heaviest superheavy nuclei. Additionally, the study of beta decays can provide access to nuclei with even neutron numbers, whereas alpha decays are limited to nuclei with even neutron numbers and odd proton numbers. Our results show that the beta decays of 4n-alpha cluster-induced nuclei are highly sensitive to the neutron-to-proton ratio. Neural machine translation systems face challenges when translating with limited computational resources, especially in scenarios with restricted memory and CPU capabilities. To address this issue, we developed a resource-efficient NMT approach that utilizes cross-modal alignment to optimize resource usage by reducing the number of parameters. By applying this method to the WMT14 English-German Shuffled dataset in a restricted memory environment, we achieved comparable translation performance to the original model, but with significantly reduced computational requirements. Moreover, we observed that our approach effectively preserves the quality of translation even at lower memory capacities as opposed to simply downsizing the model size. To further validate the effectiveness of our solution, we also applied it to the low-resource language pair Czech-English and demonstrated its ability to handle large datasets while outperforming similar models in terms of translation quality. Advances in indistinguishability-style cryptographic protocols have significantly expanded the capabilities of secure multi-party computation. However, constructive cryptography, a more recent approach, focuses on identifying attacks that can be ruled out, offering a more precise analysis of security. Yet, the development of interactive constructive protocols has been relatively slow due to a lack of foundational techniques for constructing such interactions. To address this gap, we provide a practical model for designing and analyzing interactive protocols within the constructive framework, along with sample applications. Specifically, we develop a simple updatable encryption scheme and an efficient private information retrieval protocol, both featuring strong security guarantees. This work builds upon foundational research in constructive cryptography, including the work of Mironov et al., and the subsequent work of Dodis et al. In particular, we leverage the fundamental universal simulation framework established by Mironov et al., and adapt and extend it to accommodate interactive protocols. We also utilize the cyclic notation introduced by Dodis et al. to achieve a more streamlined and efficient treatment of security proofs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of our approach by developing novel constructions, such as updatable encryption and private information retrieval protocols. These constructions are secure in the face of adversaries that can only apply computational distinguishers. We also show that these protocols can be realized in the CCA2 setting, without the need for public-key encryption. This research contributes to the development of a more refined and precise approach to security, distinct from the prevailing reduction-based approach in indistinguishability-style cryptographic protocols. We hope that it will encourage further work in the field of constructive cryptography. This study centers around the Robin Torsion problem, which involves minimizing the functional $F(u) = \int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^2 dx + u^2\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\delta_{i}$. The solution $u$ must satisfy the conditions $u=0$ on $\partial \Omega - \Gamma$, where $\Gamma$ is a portion of $\partial \Omega$ of positive measure, and $u=\phi$ on $\Gamma$, where $\phi$ is a given function in $H^1(\Omega)$. We will prove a stiffness estimate for this problem, showing that the difference between the partial derivatives of the solution and the boundary data is bounded from above by a constant times the distance between the two measures. As a result, we will also derive a maximum principle for the solution of this problem, which is a first for the Robin Torsion problem. Furthermore, we will investigate the behavior of the two measures as the coefficients of the functional approach the critical values of the Pucci-Minkowski problem. The stiffness estimate will also be generalized to a broader class of problems, including the minimal surface problem and its analog in higher dimensions. The minimal surface problem, which involves minimizing the functional $F(u) = \int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^2 dx + u^3\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\delta_{i}$, will be considered in both the Dirichlet and Robin boundary cases. The necessary proofs for these results are provided in the final section of this study. \end{abstract}

High-power lasers can cause significant damage to materials at an atomic and nanoscale level due to the rapid heating from the laser light. To better understand this process, we developed an advanced simulation method that accounts for the thermal energy in three related stages of cooling: the initial rapid cooling, the intermediate stage of lattice cooling, and the final stage of electronic cooling. Using this method, we examined how high-power laser pulses interact with silicon substrates and explored the damage that occurs at varying levels of power and duration. Our results show that the damage process depends on the stage of cooling and the power of the laser. Specifically, we found that the damage threshold is determined by the duration of the laser pulse and the power it emits. At high pulse durations of several nanoseconds or more, the damage threshold is related to the power it emits, whereas at lower pulse durations of less than 5 nanoseconds, the damage threshold is largely independent of both the power and duration. To verify these findings, we conducted a range of experiments using laser pulses with varying levels of power and duration. Our results align with the predictions from the three-stage cooling model, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the damage that occurs when high-power lasers interact with materials. This new understanding may help to develop more resilient materials and techniques for preventing laser damage. GANs have become increasingly popular for their ability to generate complex image data sets. Despite their effectiveness, GAN training is still a poorly understood area, particularly the issue of mode collapse, which remains a significant challenge even after extensive research. Mode collapse occurs when the generator produces only a limited set of possible outcomes, even after extensive training. Previous studies have attempted to address mode collapse by analyzing the distribution of the generator's output, but this approach is time-consuming and requires additional hyperparameters. This paper presents a new method to detect mode collapse by examining the Hessian eigenvalues of the generator during training, which provides a more accurate and efficient indication of mode collapse than previous techniques. Furthermore, the proposed approach is applied to different GAN architectures, including WGAN, WGAN-GP, BigGAN, and StyleGAN. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms previous detectors in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and is able to identify mode collapse in various GAN architectures, even when it is not apparent through other methods. Additionally, the proposed approach is able to identify mode collapse in a generator that has converged to produce a diverse set of possible outcomes. This paper presents empirical evidence that mode collapse is a persistent issue in GAN training, even when the generator has converged, and that the proposed method is a reliable way to identify mode collapse in such cases. Deep neural networks are vulnerable to "adversarial examples" - slightly distorted inputs that a model accurately classifies, yet looks indistinguishable from an original, intact sample. Most research on adversarial defense has centered on robust examples that consistently mislead models across various settings, despite their relatively small size in comparison to typical data sets. This paper delves into the characteristics of these examples and their susceptibility to attacks, focusing on the relative insignificance of their distortions in comparison to original data features. By examining the interplay between adversarial examples and model features, we identify a correlation between robust example generation and a specific feature subset - non-semantic features. Building on this connection, we propose a method to create more aggressive adversarial examples that leverage these non-semantic features. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in generating more aggressive adversarial examples compared to traditional methods. Additionally, we provide a more straightforward interpretation of adversarial example generation using non-semantic features, which can be utilized to improve model performance. This research contributes to the existing literature by shedding light on the characteristics of adversarial examples and proposing a novel method for generating more aggressive examples. By examining the interplay between adversarial examples and model features, we can gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon and improve model performance. This research also highlights the importance of considering non-semantic features in adversarial example generation and suggests avenues for future exploration. A novel stopping rule for Krylov methods is proposed, which replaces the traditional residual-based measure with a distance metric derived from the distance between linear systems, using the current solution as a reference point. This approach is derived from fundamental linear system properties and does not rely on extra computational costs. We demonstrate that this method converges to the solution of the underlying problem and provides guarantees on accuracy and residual norms. An extensive set of numerical experiments confirms that this method outperforms existing solutions in terms of reliability and efficiency. This new algorithm is particularly beneficial for solving linear systems with extremely small residual norms. Moreover, its efficiency is further enhanced when combined with other methods, including trust-region and line-search algorithms, for which we also propose a new iteration stopping rule. Comprehensive numerical experiments confirm that this method offers a highly reliable and efficient alternative to conventional Krylov solvers. The proposed algorithms have been implemented in the publicly available code, which can be accessed at https://github.com/jbodart/linear_solver. This code is also integrated into the MATLAB Optimization Toolbox. Specifically, the trust-region solver, mldiv, has been modified to utilize the new stopping rule, and a new solver named lscov has been created to leverage the proposed line-search algorithm. This code is also compatible with the high-performance computing environment provided by the Cray System Image for the Exascale Computing Initiative. Furthermore, the proposed methods have been used to solve a large-scale linear programming problem arising from a real-world data assimilation application. This implementation has achieved a significant reduction in computational time compared to the state-of-the-art solvers, including ipopt and ode15s. In addition, the proposed methods have been used to solve a large-scale nonlinear programming problem arising from a real-world data assimilation application. This implementation has achieved a significant reduction in computational time compared to the state-of-the-art solvers, including ipopt and fmincon. In both cases, the proposed methods have demonstrated superior performance, offering up to 1000 times faster convergence compared to the state-of-the-art solvers. This improved performance has been achieved without incurring additional computational costs. Furthermore, the proposed methods have been demonstrated to be highly scalable, achieving linear speedup on 64 processors. In summary, the proposed methods have the potential to revolutionize interior-point methods for large-scale optimization problems, both linear and nonlinear. This development is expected to lead to the creation of a new class of solvers that can efficiently tackle complex optimization problems, including those with multiple objectives and constraints.

This study examines secure transmission methods in a spectrum-sharing small-cell network, which incorporates backhaul connectivity and unreliable links for information exchange. By utilizing transmitter selection and backhaul connectivity, users can obtain channel state information, but this data may be accessed by eavesdroppers due to wireless transmission on a shared spectrum. As a result, the eavesdropper's ability to obtain information can impact security outcomes. In this context, the security threshold is defined as the rate at which an eavesdropper can obtain information. Under these conditions, the problem of transmitter selection is redefined to ensure that the chosen transmitter maintains a secure margin, but this approach is challenging due to its computationally intensive nature. To address this limitation, a new method based on the Lagrange dual problem is proposed, which can provide a lower bound on the security threshold. By iteratively optimizing the Lagrange multipliers, the method can be easily implemented with reduced complexity. Furthermore, the impact of backhaul reliability on security is analyzed, and it is shown that the backhaul quality has a significant effect on the eavesdropper's ability to obtain information. By leveraging the backhaul quality, the security threshold can be increased, and this can be achieved through joint optimization of resource allocation and backhaul quality control. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed methods, and they outperform other existing approaches in terms of security performance. Specifically, the proposed methods are up to 40% more secure compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the methods are robust and can provide a high level of security even under imperfect knowledge of channel state information. Additionally, the methods are effective in scenarios with unreliable backhaul connectivity, and they can provide a high level of security with only 20% reliable backhaul links. This is achieved through joint optimization of transmitter selection, backhaul quality control, and power allocation. Simulation results confirm the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed methods. Overall, the proposed methods provide a high level of security in various scenarios with different assumptions on channel state information, backhaul reliability, and other parameters. As a result, the proposed methods are highly suitable for practical secure transmission applications. The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/sammyhkung/SecTSEBS. The task of detecting fake news remains a pressing concern due to its inherent ambiguity and the sophisticated nature of false news creators. Current approaches rely on data-driven methods to identify fake news; however, these methods require substantial labeled data to train effectively. In an effort to address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel data generation technique for automatically labeling and producing high-quality training data for fake news detection. A key aspect of this method is the development of a generator that creates propaganda-rich content, which significantly enhances the performance of fake news detection models. To achieve this, we leverage a novel metric called Propaganda Intensity Score, which measures the level of propaganda in news content. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our data generation technique in improving the state-of-the-art fake news detection models. Additionally, our results show that the generated data can produce better results than actual, manually labeled data. Importantly, this method can be applied to various fake news detection tasks, including detecting various types of misinformation, such as false news, rumors, and biased content. Overall, this research presents a novel approach to automatically generate high-quality training data for fake news detection. To facilitate future research, we have released the code, data, and models used in this study. They are available on our GitHub repository. In this paper, we propose a novel method to create and execute Learnability Lock attacks by manipulating neural network architectures with invertible transformations. Notably, our Learnability Lock attack can have severe consequences, with some models being permanently damaged after exposure. A novel non-overlapping domain decomposition method for incompressible Stokes problems is proposed. This method is applicable to a broad range of linear elliptic systems with continuous pressure, and its convergence is theoretically proven and experimentally validated. Experimental findings indicate that the method's computational efficiency is directly proportional to the size of subdomains, but ultimately outperforms existing methods. Moreover, our proposed method is found to converge at a rate of $O(\sqrt{K})$ across subdomain kernels, and $O(K^{-1})$ in the case of a constant right-hand side, surpassing the performance of traditional Stokes-Petrov methods. In comparison studies, our proposed method demonstrated a notable reduction in the number of degrees of freedom required to achieve a comparable level of accuracy in solving incompressible Stokes problems. This method's computational efficiency is further enhanced by utilizing preconditioners, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations of complex flow problems in incompressible hydrodynamics. Overall, our proposed method is an effective and efficient numerical technique for solving incompressible Stokes problems. A related MATLAB implementation can be found at the GitHub repository "junye-Zhu/Non-Overlapping-Method-for-Incompressible-Stokes-Problems". Additionally, our research has been further documented in the dissertation "Efficient Numerical Methods for Incompressible Stokes Problems". It is worth noting that our proposed method is a pioneering work in the field of numerical Stokes problems. To the knowledge of the authors, our proposed method is the first of its kind to achieve a rate of convergence of $O(\sqrt{K})$ in solving incompressible Stokes problems. Furthermore, our research provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for this method, and its application to a broader range of linear elliptic systems with continuous pressure offers significant originality and contributions. A notable aspect of our research is the development of a novel preconditioner for the Schur complement, and its application to a broader range of linear elliptic systems with continuous pressure. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) exhibits characteristics of a cell-to-cell transmission virus, 
yet it can also be transmitted through the environment, similar to other similar viruses.
We developed an agent-based model to analyze HCV transmission in an in-vitro setting,
where the virus's lifecycle is influenced by various factors such as cell density, viral load,
and the cell's susceptibility to the virus.
We simulated two transmission pathways: direct cell-to-cell transmission and 
indirect transmission through free virus in the environment.
We found that direct cell-to-cell transmission accounts for 90% of new infections.
However, when comparing theoretical models to experimental data, we observed 
that direct cell-to-cell transmission significantly outpaces indirect transmission.
We conclude that direct cell-to-cell transmission is the primary driver of HCV 
propagation in this in-vitro setting. We provide recommendations for designing more accurate 
theoretical models and conducting further in-vitro studies to gain a deeper understanding 
of HCV transmission pathways. Ultimately, this research aims to inform the design of more 
accurate models predicting the spread of infectious diseases in various populations.

Vectorization is a crucial optimization technique that enhances the performance of processors by executing multiple operations simultaneously. This research introduces a novel approach to vectorize the CSparse matrix-multiply function, which is commonly used in various linear algebra applications. The technique applies trace analysis to identify the linear dependencies within function paths, thereby facilitating vectorization. The method is demonstrated to be effective in analyzing complex linear algebra algorithms, even when they involve intricate data structures like matrices and set data bases. Furthermore, this paper showcases the benefits of using high-level trace analysis frameworks like LLVM to vectorize recursive functions that manipulate complex data structures, particularly in optimizing performance on CPUs equipped with AVX-2 and AVX-512 capabilities. The implementation is validated by comparing its performance with the highly optimized CSparse library and achieving vectorization of benchmarked functions. Additionally, this paper presents a simple matrix-based version of the quicksort algorithm, which is vectorized and used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the trace analysis technique. The implementation is then extended to support various matrix types, including the compressed sparse row format. The vectorized implementation is finally compared with the BLAS library and found to outperform it significantly on CPUs equipped with AVX-2 technology. The goal of domain adaptation is to adapt a pre-trained model on a source domain to a new source domain or to various new domains using unlabeled data. Our study evaluates multiple domain adaptation techniques for image recognition tasks, focusing on two primary areas:  a) domain adaptation using labeled data, b) domain adaptation without labeled data. In the first case, we investigate the effectiveness of cutting-edge techniques, including Mixup, Cutmix, and Data Augmentation methods. For the second scenario, we explore the performance of self-supervised learning, specifically SimCLR and BYOL, when transferring models from ImageNet to a new source domain. Our results show that Cutmix outperforms other domain adaptation techniques, achieving an average accuracy of 85.8% on the VOC 2012 dataset, followed by Data Augmentation with 84.3% accuracy, while SimCLR and BYOL yield 74.8% and 72.7% accuracy respectively. Our findings are expected to serve as a benchmark for future research in domain adaptation techniques. The presence of extraterrestrial moons with highly eccentric orbits can lead to significant variations in their orbital distances, resulting in dynamic changes that impact their interaction with their host planets. This research investigates the influence of these eccentric orbits on the moon's tidal and orbital evolution within exoplanetary systems. We found that highly eccentric moons undergo tidal heating, causing their orbits to decay at a rate influenced by the host planet's size and tidal Q parameter. This decay process can be accelerated under certain conditions, potentially leading to moon capture in less than a billion years. In contrast, scenarios featuring planets with low tidal Q and smaller sizes may result in orbit decay times spanning millions to billions of years. Furthermore, our study reveals that orbital capture times are inversely dependent on the moon's initial eccentricity, and larger planets tend to have more circular orbits due to increased tidal heating. This research also explores the implications of dynamically changing moon orbits on the detection and characterization of extraterrestrial systems using transit techniques. Specifically, our findings suggest that highly eccentric moons can produce multiple stable states with different transit durations, potentially leading to transit duration variations and periodic changes in brightness, and may also induce periodic variations in the timing of planetary transits due to moon-induced precession. Finally, our study suggests that highly eccentric moons may be more likely to exhibit atmospheric escape and support surface liquid water under certain conditions. These results are supported by numerical simulations and case studies of exoplanetary systems. Overall, our research provides valuable insights into the orbital dynamics of highly eccentric moons and their impact on the detection and characterization of extraterrestrial systems. To address this issue, a novel method is presented for evaluating finite-temperature QCD pressure using a novel diagram arrangement. This approach involves converting the diagrams into a more manageable form by integrating temperature-related components and focusing on the remaining, more tractable graph structures. By applying this method, key contributions to the $g^6$ term have been identified and evaluated using a combination of theoretical, numerical, and analytical methods. As a result, a new, simplified equation for the QCD pressure is provided, accurate to a 1.3% margin of error for the entire range of relevant temperatures and quark masses. Furthermore, a new, simplified equation for the QCD energy density is derived, and its accuracy is verified to within 1.4% for the specified parameters. The sign problem has been a major hurdle in numerical simulations of field theory, particularly for systems with complex path integrals. A groundbreaking method called the Lefschetz thimble method has gained widespread attention for tackling this issue. This method involves redefining the integration path in field space using a more suitable geometry, allowing for accurate sampling without the sign cancellations. A comprehensive guide to the Lefschetz thimble method has been lacking, so we're filling the gap by exploring its underlying principles, high-dimensional implementation, and applications in physics. This includes detailed explanations of algorithms, various examples of its use, and further applications in physics. This study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding and promote wider adoption of the Lefschetz thimble method in physics. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that the Lefschetz thimble method has the potential to resolve the non-equivalent sampling issue affecting imaginary-time Monte Carlo simulations. This could potentially resolve a long-standing challenge in physics. Additionally, our research explores the relationship between the Lefschetz thimble method and other proposed solutions to the sign problem, such as the extended Lefschetz thimble and the transition distribution method. Current protocols for privacy protection, such as the Generalized Voronoi Partition (GVP) and its variations, have significant drawbacks. Specifically, GVP and its variants necessitate users to install client software, which incurs additional power consumption and resource requirements. Moreover, these solutions may introduce considerable delays in location updates. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel protocol leveraging edge computing to efficiently process GVP-related computations and minimize user's computational burden. This approach enables users to utilize their resources more effectively and reduces energy consumption. Furthermore, our scheme enhances location update speed by optimizing the computation at edge servers. To measure the performance of our protocol, we assess its energy consumption, computation time, and delay. This proposed solution offers a compelling alternative to traditional GVP-based protocols. Our simulation results demonstrate substantial energy savings, with reduced consumption of 59% compared to the original protocol. Additionally, significant reductions in computation time and location update delays are observed, with decreases of 77% and 75% respectively, when compared to the original protocol. These results indicate that our edge computing-based approach is a promising solution for mobile devices. This work provides valuable insights into designing efficient protocols for privacy protection and resource preservation, which are critical considerations in LBS. In large-scale distributed learning scenarios, such as healthcare, privacy concerns are alleviated through federated learning, which enables model training across multiple clients while keeping data local. Online FL extends this approach, allowing global models to be updated with mini-batches from individual clients in each round of training. Current online FL techniques rely on a single kernel, limiting their adaptability to complex data patterns. To address this issue, we introduce MKOFL, a kernel-driven method for online FL that adaptively selects multiple kernels from data features. By applying a kernel-based aggregation rule to each mini-batch from clients, MKOFL updates the global model with an effective learning rate. Our theoretical analysis confirms MKOFL's convergence and superior regret bounds compared to the state-of-the-art online FL approach, OFL. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate MKOFL's consistency with theoretical predictions and delivering the best performance among compared methods. Notably, MKOFL exhibits substantial accuracy gains, such as a 2.31% improvement on CIFAR-100 over OFL and 0.02% better accuracy on MNIST. Our proposed MKOFL approach also facilitates automatic feature selection, reducing user burden in online FL. The code for MKOFL is available at https://github.com/ChangWenZhang/MKOFL. Handwritten date identification has become a crucial task due to its numerous practical applications, including automatic document classification and enhancing information retrieval efficiency for historical newspaper transcripts. This research paper focuses on developing a handwritten date identification system for South African languages. Building on the success of a national large-scale handwriting recognition competition, we created a new dataset consisting of approximately 27,000 handwritten letters written in 57 languages, including South African languages. This dataset features a comprehensive collection of hand-written letters from various languages, with each word having been annotated with a date, genre, and language information, as well as corrected letters. A proposed system, DARE, leverages a convolutional neural network architecture to predict the genre and language of handwritten words, with its accuracy evaluated using the ROC curve and area under the curve. A detailed analysis of the dataset's distribution, model performance, and other relevant metrics are also presented, with insights into developing effective methods for improving handwritten date identification systems. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our research on the development of a South African languages handwriting recognition system. The developed dataset will be made publicly available to foster progress in handwritten date identification research. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/TUTAI2019/DARE. This study presents a dataset designed to facilitate sentiment manipulation and fine-grained emotion analysis.  The corpus comprises a vast array of documents featuring varied content types, including articles and comments.  Each entry in the dataset is paired with a primary emotion and corresponding sentiment, allowing researchers to examine the intricate connections between emotions and sentiments.  An in-depth analysis of the dataset's sentiment patterns reveals a strong correlation between emotions and sentiments, indicating that individuals tend to express certain feelings in conjunction with specific emotions.  To validate the dataset's effectiveness, a baseline model is trained on the data to achieve a maximum F1 accuracy of 0.78.  The proposed corpus offers a novel framework for researchers to explore the interplay between emotions and sentiments, potentially enhancing sentiment analysis and emotion recognition tasks. A significant concern with deploying Deep Neural Networks involves their potential to misbehave when presented with specially crafted inputs, known as Adversarial Examples, which a third-party attacker has intentionally crafted. This malicious behavior can be achieved by modifying a target model's weights, specifically introducing a backdoor, allowing an adversary to force the model to incorrectly recognize specific objects. This paper delves into the feasibility of injecting backdoors through weight modification, examining the necessary conditions and their practical implications. Specifically, it's discovered that introducing a backdoored activation function, called a Trojan Function, is possible, enabling the misbehavior to occur. However, this approach has a significant drawback: significantly increasing the training time by a factor of at least 10. Furthermore, this research explores the connection between backdoor injection and Trojan Functions through weight modification, comparing it to existing techniques. Additionally, it's found that injecting backdoors via weight modification is feasible for pre-trained models, significantly reducing their performance but allowing for backdoor injection. This paper contributes to the understanding of backdoor attacks by introducing a new method and its implications for defending against them. This research is particularly relevant in light of recent breakthroughs in backdoor attacks, specifically the Adaptive Attack, which can evade existing countermeasures. This paper's findings are expected to motivate further research and highlight the limitations of existing defense mechanisms. This research is available on the GitHub platform. Scientific data analysis is increasingly reliant on large-scale data sets, 
which are often produced by cutting-edge particle accelerators. As researchers 
work with these data sets, they require advanced tools to streamline tasks such as 
merging, aligning, and modifying these complex files in a timely manner. To 
meet this need, we have developed a parallel HDF5 dataset merging tool, which can 
merge multiple files into a single one, while also reorganize data within the 
file to optimize the analysis process. In this paper, we describe the design and 
implementation of our tool, which is written in C++ and utilizes the HDF5 library 
for handling the data inputs. To evaluate its effectiveness, we have tested our 
tool on a large dataset containing 9,000 files with physics data, and the results 
show a substantial speed increase in the merging process, enabling the creation 
of a larger dataset in a fraction of the time it would have taken in a sequential 
process. Furthermore, our tool has also been successful in reorganizing data 
within the merged file, which in turn allows for faster data access and analysis

In the field of software engineering, it's well-documented that experienced programmers are in short supply. To address this issue, various educational initiatives have been established to educate individuals with little or no programming experience. Effective instruction in this group requires a comprehensive approach incorporating text, visualizations, and code. Although research has identified the benefits of this approach, there is still a knowledge gap regarding how the brain processes different types of information. To fill this gap, we conducted a neuroimaging study involving 11 novice programmers tasked with reading, visualizing, and coding either alone or in combination. Our findings indicate that the brain's language processing network is more active when participants are introduced to new programming concepts, whereas the network responsible for spatial processing is more active in visual tasks. Notably, we discovered that the brain's default mode network is deactivated when participants are engaged in hands-on coding exercises such as writing code. These findings have significant implications for software engineering education and provide a foundation for future research to bridge the gap between cognitive performance and neurobiological markers. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate a deeper understanding of programming and learning by leveraging insights from cognitive neuroscience. By doing so, we hope to improve educational effectiveness and enhance student learning outcomes. The study's results are publicly available, and our goal is to encourage future research in this area. By compressing a complex system into a more compact representation while preserving essential connectivity, the proposed method facilitates accurate state estimation. Image dehazing is a significant challenge in computer vision due to the numerous applications requiring it, such as autonomous driving and security. Current methods primarily focus on recovering details from the transparent sky while overlooking the complexities in hazy images caused by multiple factors. This paper introduces a novel, efficient model called Rich Feature Extraction with Feature Affinity Module (RF-EFA) that can accurately restore hazy images in a computationally efficient manner. By incorporating feature affinity, the model captures the complex relationships between hazy and clear images, enabling it to simulate clear transmission paths. Furthermore, the model extracts rich semantic information from the hazy images using a feature affinity-based attention mechanism. As a result, the model can accurately reconstruct the transmission paths and recover the lost details in hazy images. The proposed model can handle both single-image dehazing and video dehazing, demonstrating superior performance on both single-image dehazy datasets (IHT-10K, TO92) and video dehazy datasets (VSD-1M) in our experiments. In the realm of speedrunning, players aim to execute intricate sequences of actions at an exceptionally high pace within a given game, often pushing the limits of what is considered feasible. Traditionally, this feat is achieved by humans, but recent advancements have led to a growing interest in automating these processes. This study provides an introduction to speedrunning navigation and assesses existing research on automation, offering a comprehensive perspective on what is presently known. Furthermore, it highlights areas for potential investigation in the realm of automated speedruns. Two prominent frameworks, Twiddle and VWAA, are introduced, and a demonstration is presented on how these tools can expedite the creation of a VWAA navigation route. Finally, a discussion is made on the benefits and drawbacks of automating speedruns, along with the potential challenges that may arise from doing so in the near future. This study is available as a book chapter in the forthcoming book "Human-Machine Cooperation in Games".

The emergence of new viral variants is often driven by their ability to evade the host's immune system, which in turn has driven the development of antiviral therapies. Researchers have successfully used computational methods to model and predict viral behavior, with a notable example being the COVID-19 pandemic where existing vaccines failed to protect against certain SARS-CoV-2 variants. AI-driven prediction models have shown potential in forecasting viral behavior and identifying vulnerable populations before the emergence of new variants, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we propose a new class of AI models that incorporate topological features, specifically deep persistent homology, to predict future viral variants. By analyzing the host-virus interaction network, we demonstrate that our approach can accurately forecast the emergence of new variants up to 6 months in advance. Furthermore, we show that our model can be used to identify potential new variants that may arise as a result of mutations in specific genes, providing valuable insights for the development of effective treatments and vaccines. Our findings suggest that incorporating topological features into AI models can enhance their predictive accuracy and provide a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms that drive viral evolution. This work opens up new possibilities for using topological AI to monitor the COVID-19 pandemic and other infectious diseases, and to develop effective strategies for prevention and control. A key distinguishing feature of this search is the inclusion of a top quark pair in the final state, making it an ideal candidate for a deeper analysis of the existing CMS data. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we have developed a new set of kinematic variables designed to enhance the sensitivity to top partner signals, which can be employed to refine mass splittings and production cross-sections in top squark and topino models. Furthermore, we have investigated the feasibility of leveraging top quark pair final states to set limits on SUSY parameters in top squark models, with a particular focus on the top squark-neutralino associated production channel. While the search for top squark pair events has the potential to yield more stringent mass limits, the current analysis is constrained by the limited sensitivity to top squark masses below 400 GeV, which can be attributed to the substantial background from top quark pair production. A related study involving top quark pair plus photon events has also been conducted, which has enabled the derivation of mass limits for wino-like light neutralinos. Notably, the current analysis has yielded a bound on the mass of the light neutralino of 115 GeV, which represents a significant improvement over existing bounds. A key finding of this study is the observation that a top quark pair final state search can be effectively integrated with existing searches for top squark pair events in the top quark-rich final state, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the SUSY spectrum. A particular example of this is the simultaneous analysis of top squark pair and top quark pair plus photon events, which has enabled the extension of the current mass limits for wino-like light neutralinos to 120 GeV. A key takeaway from this study is the realization that a top quark pair final state search can be utilized to refine the existing understanding of the SUSY parameter space, particularly in the context of top squark and topino models. Quantum entropies serve as effective tools for analyzing the behavior of quantum systems. Our study also demonstrates the existence of unitary operators with minimal and maximal uncertainty and introduces a novel concept of sub-operators, which offers an alternative perspective on operator uncertainty. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of a framework for entropic uncertainty measures in quantum operators. The findings have the potential to facilitate novel applications within the context of quantum information theory. Secondly, we developed a more realistic assumption about information exchange, where individuals receive multiple pieces of opposing information, rather than just a single piece as in prior research. Thirdly, we developed a method for simulating the evolution of opinions in large groups, where individuals interact with a limited number of neighbors, offering or rejecting competing perspectives. Our findings also revealed that individuals' opinions are shaped by both the quality of information they receive and the structure of their social networks, with network topology exerting the greatest influence on opinion formation. Furthermore, we found that individuals tend to converge to the majority view within their social networks, but this is also influenced by the quality of information, with high-quality information potentially leading to the majority adopting that perspective even if it's not the network consensus. This research introduces AppealNet, a highly efficient and accurate edge/cloud collaborative system for deep neural networks. AppealNet's innovative edge inference approach involves appealing to the cloud for complex layers when resources are insufficient, whereas it processes lighter layers at the edge to minimize latency. AppealNet's distinct feature is its decision-making layer prioritization strategy, which optimizes efficiency and accuracy by carefully selecting layers to be computed at the edge and the cloud. Our experiments demonstrate AppealNet's ability to reduce inference latency by up to 32% compared to traditional methods while achieving comparable or superior accuracy. Additionally, AppealNet's architecture can be easily scaled to handle various network configurations, demonstrating its potential to outperform current best-in-class methods. OG-SPACE can be customized to fit various growth patterns, cell division rules, and genetic mutation rules, enabling researchers to analyze large genetic mutation data sets. Its performance has been validated by comparing it with a comprehensive simulation approach, demonstrating its ability to provide accurate results in a reasonable timeframe. We introduce the ASR2K challenge, aiming to develop a single, universal speech
recognition system for nearly 2000 languages with minimal, representative
audio requirements. A novel evaluation framework is developed to simulate end-to-end
speech recognition for unseen languages and unknown speakers through a zero-data approach.
This framework is put to test using 3,400 audio recordings from languages with limited or no prior
speech recognition research. A comprehensive comparison is conducted between two ASR models: one
trained on extensive multilingual datasets and another trained on a smaller, multilingual dataset.
Results demonstrate that the latter performs surprisingly well, achieving an average character error
rate of 59.9% on the unseen data, highlighting the potential of a zero-data approach to expand
ASR capabilities to previously underserved languages and dialects. ASR2K resources and further details
can be found at https://asr2k.github.io. This research is part of a community-driven initiative. A
special issue for ASR2K is currently under review in the Computational Linguistics journal. Contributions
to the ASR2K project are welcome and can be submitted via https://asr2k.github.io/contribute. Join the
discussions on the ASR2k community at https://discord.com/invite/Nq7KX7gK. Donate your time, expertise,

Conversely, a time-limited warning system encouraged them to prioritize areas of the object that drew their attention rather than their periphery. We applied this framework to a study where 26 participants interacted with a mid-level autopilot system in a 20-minute flight simulation, and measured their trust in the system throughout the mission. Federated learning, specifically customized federated learning (CFL), addresses the issue of diverse client data sets in a multi-client, single-server framework by allowing different clients to develop personalized models. A key challenge in CFL is achieving a unified global level of performance across various client models, as localized client data sets can lead to sub-optimal results. To address this challenge, CFL frameworks often rely on a single optimization method, limiting their effectiveness. To address this limitation, we propose a new CFL approach that utilizes hypernetworks, a secondary network that generates the primary model's parameters. Our approach allows for a more efficient and scalable optimization process, enabling the simultaneous training of multiple clients. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that our CFL framework can achieve a unified global level of performance across various client models. Pretrained multilingual language models, such as Multilingual BERT (mBERT), enable the analysis of low-resource or endangered languages by leveraging knowledge from high-resource languages within the same language family. This ability is crucial for understanding how languages influence predictions, especially in cross-lingual tasks. Our research focuses on the dependency between language properties and mBERT's cross-lingual capabilities. We investigate how mBERT's internal language representation affects its performance in cross-lingual tasks, such as predicting part-of-speech tags and sentiment. Our findings reveal a correlation between language similarity, mBERT's internal language representation, and the model's performance in various languages. Specifically, languages with similar representation in mBERT exhibit better outcomes in cross-lingual tasks, such as part-of-speech tagging and sentiment analysis. To further explore this phenomenon, we developed a novel approach called First Align, then Forecast (LATF), which involves two steps. It first aligns mBERT's hidden representations of two languages and then uses the resulting alignment matrix to predict the target language. Our results show that LATF significantly outperforms the baseline model, such as xLM-Multilingual-Large, in cross-lingual tasks, especially in languages with limited similarity to the reference language. Our study contributes to the development of language models for diverse languages and sheds light on the inner workings of multilingual language representations. This research may inspire the creation of language models for languages with limited data and the analysis of language similarity in neural machine translation. analyzing local image features and utilizing currents as a measure of object 
salience. Our method diverges from existing current-based techniques by drawing 
inspiration from the fact that neural networks can detect and respond to

saliency map through a generalized Morlet wavelet transform. This approach is 
evaluated against leading current-based saliency detection methods, demonstrating 
superior results. Furthermore, our method is shown to outperform other top 
approaches, including the use of deep neural networks for local image analysis.

development of more advanced saliency detection techniques grounded in image data.

Experimental results demonstrate LATTE's ability to achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on a range of language tasks while requiring less computational and memory resources. Furthermore, LATTE's modular design and layer configuration flexibility allow it to adapt to various input sequences and tasks, making it a more versatile model. Ultimately, LATTE's ability to train multiple transformer-based models within a single network can lead to more efficient training and inference processes. This paper explores the use of active learning in classification tasks, specifically how to select unlabeled samples to annotate efficiently. The key issue is that existing active learning methods often prioritize the most informative unlabeled samples without considering the potential impact on the model's performance with the annotated data. The theoretical analysis shows that our approach can be cast as a linear programming problem, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on large-scale image classification tasks, achieving substantial improvements over other methods in terms of efficiency and performance. This study introduces the principles of a novel garbage collector called Version Driven Reclamation (VBR), which employs a straightforward yet effective method to manage memory allocation and garbage removal within concurrent programs. VBR assigns a unique identifier to each software version, allowing it to determine which data versions should be erased. As the system continuously updates this identifier, it can accurately reclaim outdated memory space without causing program crashes related to lost version information. Unlike existing approaches, VBR does not require explicit user intervention or program modifications. Experimental findings demonstrate that VBR, when paired with a simple block-based memory design, achieves exceptional performance outcomes, including improved speed, lower energy consumption, and reduced data transfer during garbage collection. These results position VBR as a superior solution for efficient memory management in real-time systems. Given its capabilities, VBR is an attractive option for future systems that demand reliable and efficient memory management. Simulation results indicate that VBR outperforms other collectors, such as Java's garbage collector, in terms of power usage while maintaining acceptable response times. By integrating VBR into modern operating systems, it is possible to significantly enhance system reliability and efficiency. This research provides the foundational concepts of VBR, along with its implementation and evaluation. Future studies can build upon these findings to further optimize this innovative approach. We investigate the distribution of entanglement across quantum field operators, 
focusing on a simplified scenario involving a massless scalar field to understand 
how operator products generate entanglement in the vacuum state. Through analytical
methods, we demonstrate that in such a system, a product of two field operators 
leading to a positive expectation value must be composed of a combination of 
positive and negative frequency fields. However, certain products of a smaller number 
of field operators may exhibit negative expectation values regardless of their 
composition of positive and negative frequency fields. Our analysis also reveals that 
the distribution of entanglement is not consistently predictable across different 
quantum states, such as the coherent state, with some states not exhibiting entanglement 
despite the presence of products of field operators that suggest otherwise. 
Consequently, our results suggest that quantum field operators, comprising both 
positive and negative frequency fields, have the capacity to store entanglement. 
We further explore the implications of these findings in the context of an extended 
interpretation of the Hilbert space and a modified understanding of what constitutes 
quantum correlations. 
The discussion also extends to the application of these findings in the study of 
interacting scalar field theories. 
Ultimately, our research offers a fresh perspective on the concept of entanglement 
in the realm of quantum field theory. 
Additionally, our results have implications for the study of entanglement in the 
distribution of particles across large distances. 
The broader significance of our findings is relevant to the study of quantum 
correlations in the presence of non-trivial spacetime configurations, such as 
cosmological spacetimes.

The task of identifying films from various sources is known as film recognition. Traditionally, this task is addressed by extracting relevant information from film captions and then classifying them. However, this method's effectiveness can be compromised by the limited availability of annotated film texts. To overcome this challenge, researchers have explored alternative approaches that utilize visual cues for film recognition. These methods typically involve creating film categorization models, which classify film images into predefined categories. While the film recognition task shares similarities with the broader goal of general image classification, existing film-based datasets are not well-suited for this task. To bridge this gap, we propose a new film recognition dataset called FilmC, which consists of 150,000 images of films from 1,600 unique categories. Our dataset is publicly available for research purposes. To improve film recognition capabilities, we propose a new approach called Film-CL that leverages vision-language representations to predict film categories. Film-CL involves a two-stage classification process, where the first stage involves predicting film categories using a pre-trained vision-language model, and the second stage involves predicting film subcategories using a classifier. Our experiments demonstrate that Film-CL outperforms traditional film recognition methods in film recognition tasks. Additionally, we show that by fine-tuning a pre-trained vision-language model on our FilmC dataset, we can obtain state-of-the-art results on various downstream film recognition tasks. A critical challenge in quantum computing is maintaining the stability of quantum states. To address this issue, we've developed a new approach that uses convergent reinforcement learning to control continuous, multi-dimensional quantum systems. By creating a self-organizing mechanism within the quantum computer, we can effectively solve a related problem known as the multi-armed bandit, enabling the computer to adapt to new quantum states. Through simulations, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach in managing the decay of qubits into the 0-state and stabilizing the computational states of a quantum majority vote. This innovative method has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of quantum computers operating in noisy environments. Furthermore, its self-optimizing capabilities make it an attractive solution for managing complex quantum systems. To facilitate future research, we've released the source code for this quantum computer on GitHub. Additionally, we've conducted a comprehensive analysis of the approach, highlighting its potential limitations and areas for further improvement. This novel framework not only addresses a critical challenge in quantum computing but also has broader implications for managing complex systems. By leveraging this approach, we can improve the reliability of quantum computers and expand their capabilities to accommodate increasingly complex applications. This study examines the problem of state estimation in power networks, which are modeled by nonlinear differential-algebraic equations. Due to the presence of nonlinearity and the presence of cross-coupling between differential states and algebraic variables, this issue is computationally challenging. To address this complexity, we develop a dynamic assessment framework, which leverages the theory of cross-coupling to evaluate the performance of various nonlinear state estimators. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework on a two-bus power network benchmark and evaluate multiple estimation methods, including full-order Kalman filters, reduced-order Kalman filters, and nonlinear state estimators. The results show that only certain nonlinear estimators and both full- and reduced-order Kalman filters are able to accurately track the system's nonlinear dynamics. However, the performance of the reduced-order Kalman filters is significantly inferior to that of the full-order Kalman filters, which underscores the importance of the cross-coupling information in achieving optimal estimation accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the state estimators can be trained offline and then validated on new, unseen data, which suggests that the estimators can be effectively applied to new network scenarios. We believe that the proposed framework will be instrumental in evaluating nonlinear state estimators for power network applications. The associated data and code for this study are available at https://github.com/Chirag-Modi/UCLAMRA. 

Keywords: Power networks, Nonlinear state estimation, Cross-coupling, State assessment, Model validation, Machine learning.

To accelerate neural architecture search, researchers utilize various techniques that employ Bayesian optimization or evolutionary algorithms to identify optimal neural architectures based on predefined search spaces. Go's concurrent design has made it a preferred choice in cloud and container applications for multiple programming languages. However, the increasing complexity of Go programs has increased the likelihood of concurrency bugs, which can lead to severe consequences. To address this issue, we have developed a novel concurrency bug detector called BinGo, which leverages binary analysis to identify bugs in Go programs. BinGo works by creating an abstract graph model of the program's control flow and detecting potential concurrency issues through system call analysis and semantic reasoning. To improve its efficiency, we have implemented a dynamic slicing technique to reduce the scope of the analysis and eliminate unnecessary information. Our evaluation results show that BinGo is able to detect a range of concurrency bugs, including synchronization issues, race conditions, and resource leaks, across various Go programs with a high level of accuracy. Furthermore, our study highlights the potential for binary analysis to be applied to other complex concurrency scenarios beyond Go programs.
